```text
domain:
    # Spatial domain is an n x n grid; time has TSTEPS steps.
    n:        size parameter (N)
    t:        dim in [0, TSTEPS)          # time
    i, j:     dims in [0, n)              # space (row i, column j)

data:
    # Conceptual C layout is u[i][j]; we choose row-major layout:
    #   offset(i,j) = i * n + j
    # Note: v, p, q are scratch arrays of the same shape.
    u[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * n + j
    v[i, j]: scratch num_t = (i, j) -> i * n + j
    p[i, j]: scratch num_t = (i, j) -> i * n + j
    q[i, j]: scratch num_t = (i, j) -> i * n + j

parameters:
    # Problem sizes:
    n:        int
    TSTEPS:   int

    # Physical/ADI coefficients (constant over i,j,t):
    DX   = 1 / n
    DY   = 1 / n
    DT   = 1 / TSTEPS
    B1   = 2
    B2   = 1
    mul1 = B1 * DT / (DX * DX)
    mul2 = B2 * DT / (DY * DY)

    a = -mul1 / 2
    b = 1 + mul1
    c0 = a                 # rename to avoid confusion with index "c"
    d = -mul2 / 2
    e = 1 + mul2
    f0 = d

    # Hoisted compound constants to avoid recomputing in inner loops:
    one_plus_2d = 1 + 2 * d
    one_plus_2a = 1 + 2 * a

    # Tuning parameters for cache/parallelism:
    TI: int  # tile size along the line index i (e.g. 64)
    # On a 32‑core CPU, TI can be chosen so that ceil((n-2)/TI) ≈ #HW threads.

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization: u[i][j] = (i + n - j) / n
    # (Matches init_array: C u[i][j] -> Buffer u(j, i))
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    for i, j:
        u[i, j] = (i + n - j) / n

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Time stepping: ADI scheme
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):           # time loop is strictly sequential

        # ========================================================
        # 1) Column sweep: solve tridiagonal systems along j for v(·, i)
        #    (each column i is independent and can be processed in parallel)
        # ========================================================

        for i in [1, n-1):               # 1 .. n-2, unordered → parallelizable
            # Boundary conditions for this column i:
            v[0,      i] = 1.0
            p[i, 0]      = 0.0
            q[i, 0]      = v[0, i]

            # Forward sweep along j (tridiagonal factorization & RHS update).
            # Data dependencies are only along j (p[i, j-1] -> p[i, j] and
            # q[i, j-1] -> q[i, j]), so this loop must remain sequential.
            for j in seq([1, n-1)):      # 1 .. n-2
                denom = a * p[i, j-1] + b
                p[i, j] = -c0 / denom

                # q[i,j] =
                #   (-d * u[j-1][i]
                #    + (1 + 2*d) * u[j][i]
                #    - f0 * u[j+1][i]
                #    - a * q[i][j-1]) /
                #   (a * p[i][j-1] + b);
                num =      -d          * u[j-1, i] \
                      + one_plus_2d    * u[j,   i] \
                      - f0             * u[j+1, i] \
                      - a              * q[i, j-1]
                q[i, j] = num / denom

            # Boundary at j = n-1:
            v[n-1, i] = 1.0

            # Backward substitution along j (uses p[i,j], q[i,j]):
            for j in seq([1, n-1)) descending:   # j = n-2 .. 1
                # v[j][i] = p[i][j] * v[j+1][i] + q[i][j];
                v[j, i] = p[i, j] * v[j+1, i] + q[i, j]

        # At this point, v holds the intermediate solution at time t
        # after the implicit solve in the "vertical" direction.

        # ========================================================
        # 2) Row sweep: solve tridiagonal systems along j for u(i, ·)
        #    (each row i is independent and can be processed in parallel)
        # ========================================================

        for i in [1, n-1):               # 1 .. n-2, unordered → parallelizable
            # Boundary conditions along row i:
            u[i, 0] = 1.0
            p[i, 0] = 0.0
            q[i, 0] = u[i, 0]

            # Forward sweep along j (tridiagonal factorization & RHS update)
            # Dependencies are again only along j.
            for j in seq([1, n-1)):      # 1 .. n-2
                denom = d * p[i, j-1] + e
                p[i, j] = -f0 / denom

                # q[i,j] =
                #   (-a * v[i-1][j]
                #    + (1 + 2*a) * v[i][j]
                #    - c0 * v[i+1][j]
                #    - d * q[i][j-1]) /
                #   (d * p[i][j-1] + e);
                num =      -a          * v[i-1, j] \
                      + one_plus_2a    * v[i,   j] \
                      - c0             * v[i+1, j] \
                      - d              * q[i, j-1]
                q[i, j] = num / denom

            # Boundary at j = n-1:
            u[i, n-1] = 1.0

            # Backward substitution along j:
            for j in seq([1, n-1)) descending:    # j = n-2 .. 1
                # u[i][j] = p[i][j] * u[i][j+1] + q[i][j];
                u[i, j] = p[i, j] * u[i, j+1] + q[i, j]

dependencies:
    # Column sweep forward pass (for each fixed t, i):
    for i in [1, n-1), j in [1, n-1):
        p(i, j-1) -> p(i, j)
        q(i, j-1) -> q(i, j)

    # Column sweep backward pass (for each fixed t, i):
    for i in [1, n-1), j in [1, n-1):
        v(j+1, i) -> v(j, i)

    # Row sweep forward pass (for each fixed t, i):
    for i in [1, n-1), j in [1, n-1):
        p(i, j-1) -> p(i, j)
        q(i, j-1) -> q(i, j)

    # Row sweep backward pass (for each fixed t, i):
    for i in [1, n-1), j in [1, n-1):
        u(i, j+1) -> u(i, j)

    # Time stepping: each step reads and writes u, v; steps are strictly ordered.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1]:
        (all updates at time t) -> (all updates at time t+1)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelism over independent lines
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # For a fixed time step t, each column in the column sweep
    # and each row in the row sweep is independent. We can exploit
    # data parallelism over i:
    #
    #   - The j-loops are left sequential due to tridiagonal
    #     recurrence dependencies along j.
    #   - u and v are only read in the respective sweep; there
    #     are no write–write conflicts across different i.
    #
    parallelize(i)  # apply to the outer i-loop in both sweeps for each t

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Blocking of the line index i
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # To better utilize caches and control per-thread work granularity,
    # we tile i into blocks of size TI and parallelize across blocks:
    #
    #   i in [1, n-1)  →  I_outer in [0, ceil((n-2)/TI)),
    #                       i_inner in [0, TI)
    #   with physical index i = 1 + I_outer * TI + i_inner,
    #   clamped to i < n-1.
    #
    block(i, I_outer, TI)
    parallelize(I_outer)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Register-local temporaries and expression hoisting
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Inside the inner j-sweeps:
    #
    # - Use scalar temporaries (registers) for:
    #       denom = a * p[i, j-1] + b
    #       denom2 = d * p[i, j-1] + e
    #   to avoid recomputing them multiple times per iteration.
    #
    # - Hoist the constant combinations:
    #       one_plus_2d = 1 + 2*d
    #       one_plus_2a = 1 + 2*a
    #   outside all loops (already reflected in 'parameters' and
    #   used in 'computation'), reducing per-iteration flops.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop unrolling of short recurrences
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # The forward/backward j-sweeps are long but fully sequential; we
    # can reduce branch and loop-control overhead by modest unrolling:
    #
    #   - Unroll j by a small factor (e.g., 2 or 4) in both the
    #     forward and backward j-loops.
    #   - This preserves the j-dependencies but presents more work
    #     per iteration to the compiler and can improve ILP.
    #
    unroll(j, 2)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Memory layout considerations
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    #   - p and q are laid out row-major in (i, j), with loops
    #     structured as 'for i { for j { ... p[i,j] ... } }', giving
    #     contiguous access along j for both column and row sweeps.
    #
    #   - u and v are accessed with neighbors in the other dimension
    #     (e.g., u[j-1, i], u[j, i], u[j+1, i] in the column sweep),
    #     which is inherently strided under any 2D dense layout. We
    #     keep a simple row-major layout and rely on caches and
    #     hardware prefetching; the added complexity and memory
    #     footprint of maintaining transposed copies would exceed the
    #     allowed 50% overhead or complicate the kernel substantially.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Summary
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # The optimized kernel:
    #   - Preserves the exact ADI update semantics and boundary
    #     conditions.
    #   - Exploits outer-loop parallelism over independent lines (i).
    #   - Tiles i for cache locality and tuning on multicore CPUs.
    #   - Hoists invariant arithmetic and uses register temporaries.
    #   - Optionally unrolls the 1D recurrences in j to increase ILP.
```

```text
domain:
    # Grid and time dimensions
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)          # time steps, sequential
    i: dim in [0, N)               # first spatial index
    j: dim in [0, N)               # second spatial index

data:
    # Row-major layout: element [i, j] is stored at i * N + j
    u[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # primary state, updated every time step
    v[i, j]: tmp   num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # intermediate state for column sweep
    # 1D temporaries for tridiagonal solves (Thomas algorithm), reused across i and sweeps.
    # These will be allocated per parallel worker (thread) to avoid races.
    p_line[j]: tmp num_t = (j) -> j             # local "p" coefficients along a line
    q_line[j]: tmp num_t = (j) -> j             # local "q" coefficients along a line

parameters:
    # Problem sizes
    N:       int      # grid dimension
    TSTEPS:  int      # number of time steps

    # PDE / scheme parameters (as in the original code)
    DX:   num_t  # = 1.0 / N
    DY:   num_t  # = 1.0 / N
    DT:   num_t  # = 1.0 / TSTEPS
    B1:   num_t  # = 2.0
    B2:   num_t  # = 1.0
    mul1: num_t  # = B1 * DT / (DX * DX)
    mul2: num_t  # = B2 * DT / (DY * DY)

    # Coefficients of the 1D implicit systems (constant over time and space)
    a: num_t  # = -mul1 / 2
    b: num_t  # =  1 + mul1
    c: num_t  # =  a
    d: num_t  # = -mul2 / 2
    e: num_t  # =  1 + mul2
    f: num_t  # =  d

    # Precomputed central coefficients to avoid recomputing 1 + 2*a, 1 + 2*d in inner loops
    center_d: num_t  # = 1 + 2 * d
    center_a: num_t  # = 1 + 2 * a

    # Tuning parameters for optimization (chosen for the target machine)
    I_TILE:    int   # tile size along i (e.g., 64)
    VEC_WIDTH: int   # SIMD width along i (e.g., 8 for AVX2 on float)


computation:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization: u[i][j] = (i + N - j) / N
    # (Matches init_array but written in natural [i, j] order.)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    init_u:
        for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            u[i, j] = (num_t(i) + num_t(N - j)) / num_t(N)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Time stepping loop: ADI scheme
    # Each step consists of a column sweep (updating v) followed
    # by a row sweep (updating u).
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    time_loop:
        for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):

            # ==========================
            # 1) Column sweep (solve along "j" for each fixed i)
            # ==========================
            col_sweep:
                # For each i in interior [1, N-2]:
                for i in [1, N-1):

                    # Boundary conditions for v and initial conditions for p,q on this line (fixed i)
                    col_bc_left:
                        v[0, i]     = num_t(1.0)   # v[0][i] = 1
                        p_line[0]   = num_t(0.0)   # p[i][0] = 0
                        q_line[0]   = v[0, i]      # q[i][0] = v[0][i]

                    # Forward sweep along j = 1..N-2
                    col_forward:
                        for j in seq([1, N-1)):    # j in [1, N-2]
                            # denom = a * p[i][j-1] + b
                            denom_col = a * p_line[j - 1] + b

                            # p[i][j] = -c / denom
                            p_line[j] = -c / denom_col

                            # q[i][j] =
                            #   (-d * u[j-1][i]
                            #    + (1 + 2*d) * u[j][i]
                            #    - f * u[j+1][i]
                            #    - a * q[i][j-1]) / denom
                            num_col = (-d * u[j - 1, i]
                                       + center_d * u[j, i]
                                       - f * u[j + 1, i]
                                       - a * q_line[j - 1])
                            q_line[j] = num_col / denom_col

                    # Right boundary for v on this line
                    col_bc_right:
                        v[N - 1, i] = num_t(1.0)   # v[N-1][i] = 1

                    # Back substitution along j = N-2..1 (descending)
                    col_backward:
                        for j in seq((N - 2) down_to 1):
                            # v[j][i] = p[i][j] * v[j+1][i] + q[i][j]
                            v[j, i] = p_line[j] * v[j + 1, i] + q_line[j]

            # ==========================
            # 2) Row sweep (solve along "j" for each fixed i)
            #     using v as the "input" and updating u.
            # ==========================
            row_sweep:
                for i in [1, N - 1):

                    # Boundary and initial conditions for u and p,q on this line (fixed i)
                    row_bc_left:
                        u[i, 0]     = num_t(1.0)   # u[i][0] = 1
                        p_line[0]   = num_t(0.0)   # p[i][0] = 0
                        q_line[0]   = u[i, 0]      # q[i][0] = u[i][0]

                    # Forward sweep along j = 1..N-2
                    row_forward:
                        for j in seq([1, N - 1)):  # j in [1, N-2]
                            # denom = d * p[i][j-1] + e
                            denom_row = d * p_line[j - 1] + e

                            # p[i][j] = -f / denom
                            p_line[j] = -f / denom_row

                            # q[i][j] =
                            #   (-a * v[i-1][j]
                            #    + (1 + 2*a) * v[i][j]
                            #    - c * v[i+1][j]
                            #    - d * q[i][j-1]) / denom
                            num_row = (-a * v[i - 1, j]
                                       + center_a * v[i, j]
                                       - c * v[i + 1, j]
                                       - d * q_line[j - 1])
                            q_line[j] = num_row / denom_row

                    # Right boundary for u on this line
                    row_bc_right:
                        u[i, N - 1] = num_t(1.0)   # u[i][N-1] = 1

                    # Back substitution along j = N-2..1 (descending)
                    row_backward:
                        for j in seq((N - 2) down_to 1):
                            # u[i][j] = p[i][j] * u[i][j+1] + q[i][j]
                            u[i, j] = p_line[j] * u[i, j + 1] + q_line[j]


dependencies:
    # Time steps are strictly sequential
    for t in [0, TSTEPS - 1]:
        time_loop(t) -> time_loop(t + 1)

    # Within a single time step:
    # Column sweep must complete before row sweep (row sweep uses v)
    for any t:
        col_sweep(t) -> row_sweep(t)

    # 1D tridiagonal structure per line (fixed i), forward and backward passes
    # Column sweep forward recurrence along j
    for any t, i, j in [1, N - 2]:
        p_line(j - 1) -> p_line(j)
        q_line(j - 1) -> q_line(j)

    # Column sweep backward recurrence along j
    for any t, i, j in [1, N - 2]:
        v(j + 1, i) -> v(j, i)

    # Row sweep forward recurrence along j
    for any t, i, j in [1, N - 2]:
        p_line(j - 1) -> p_line(j)
        q_line(j - 1) -> q_line(j)

    # Row sweep backward recurrence along j
    for any t, i, j in [1, N - 2]:
        u(i, j + 1) -> u(i, j)


optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 0) Scalar algebraic optimizations (cheap but important)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # - Hoist computation of DX, DY, DT, mul1, mul2, a..f, center_a, center_d
    #   outside all loops; they are invariant with respect to t, i, j.
    # - Reuse 'denom_col' and 'denom_row' for both p_line and q_line updates
    #   (already done in the computation section).
    # These are reflected in the 'parameters' section and in the way we wrote the computation.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 1) Reduce memory footprint and improve locality for p and q
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Original code uses 2D arrays p[i][j], q[i][j] of size N x N.
    # Here we model them as 1D temporaries p_line[j], q_line[j] that live only
    # for a single line (fixed i). We:
    #  - allocate p_line and q_line of length N per parallel worker (thread),
    #    to avoid write conflicts;
    #  - reuse them for both column and row sweeps within a time step.
    #
    # This reduces storage from O(N^2) to O(N * num_threads) and improves cache
    # locality, while preserving the mathematical result for u and v.
    # (v and u are unchanged; p and q are scratch only.)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 2) Exploit parallelism across independent lines (dimension i)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # For each time step and each sweep, lines with different i are independent:
    #  - Column sweep: for fixed t, all pairs (i1 != i2) do not depend on each other.
    #  - Row sweep: same.
    # Only recurrences along j must remain sequential.
    #
    # We tile 'i' to improve cache reuse and parallel scheduling granularity.
    # I_TILE is a tunable parameter (e.g., 32–128; 64 is a good starting point).
    #
    # We introduce separate tile indices for column and row sweeps (I_c, I_r)
    # so we can schedule them identically but independently.

    # Column sweep: outer loop over tiles of i, parallel across tiles.
    block(i, I_c, I_TILE)       # i = I_c * I_TILE + i (within col_sweep)
    parallelize(I_c)            # run different i-tiles in parallel threads

    # Row sweep: same tiling and parallelization.
    block(i, I_r, I_TILE)       # i = I_r * I_TILE + i (within row_sweep)
    parallelize(I_r)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 3) Improve SIMD utilization by vectorizing along i
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Within a fixed time step and a fixed j, computations for different i
    # are independent (no i-dependence in recurrences), so we can safely
    # vectorize across i. To make i the innermost loop:
    #
    #  - For the forward sweeps (col_forward, row_forward), interchange the
    #    i and j loops so that we iterate j sequentially in the outer loop,
    #    and i in the inner loop.
    #
    #  - For the backward sweeps (col_backward, row_backward), similarly
    #    interchange so that the descending j loop is outer, and i inner.
    #
    # This preserves the j-recursions (which remain outer and sequential)
    # while exposing a SIMD-friendly inner loop over i.

    # Column sweep forward pass:
    interchange(j, i) in col_forward   # loops become: for j (seq) { for i { ... } }
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in col_forward

    # Column sweep backward pass:
    interchange(j, i) in col_backward  # loops become: for j (seq, descending) { for i { ... } }
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in col_backward

    # Row sweep forward pass:
    interchange(j, i) in row_forward
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in row_forward

    # Row sweep backward pass:
    interchange(j, i) in row_backward
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in row_backward

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 4) Cache-friendly blocking in j (optional, conservative)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # The recurrences along j prevent parallelization across j, but we can still
    # block j to improve spatial locality when N is large. This keeps execution
    # order along j sequential while working on smaller j-ranges that fit better
    # in cache. Because dependencies are only on j-1 (forward) or j+1 (backward),
    # simple forward-order blocks are safe.
    #
    # J_TILE is another tunable parameter (e.g., 64 or 128).
    #
    # block(j, J_c, J_TILE) in col_forward
    # block(j, J_c, J_TILE) in row_forward
    # # Backward passes: same blocking but j runs in descending order within each block.
    # block(j, J_c, J_TILE) in col_backward
    # block(j, J_c, J_TILE) in row_backward

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 5) Small-loop unrolling for boundary updates
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # The boundary-setting loops are short and simple. Unrolling them can
    # slightly reduce overhead and enable better instruction scheduling.
    #
    # unroll(j, 2) in col_bc_left
    # unroll(j, 2) in col_bc_right
    # unroll(j, 2) in row_bc_left
    # unroll(j, 2) in row_bc_right

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Notes on correctness
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # - All recurrences along j remain in sequential 'seq' loops after
    #   blocking and interchange; we never parallelize or vectorize j.
    # - Parallelism and vectorization are only along i (and its tile indices),
    #   which are independent across lines.
    # - Replacing 2D p,q with 1D p_line,q_line does not change u or v,
    #   since p,q are purely temporary and never used outside their lines
    #   or time steps.
    # - Memory usage is reduced vs. the original: we remove O(N^2) storage
    #   for p and q and replace it with O(N * num_threads).
```

domain:
    # Grid is N x N, indexed by (i, j).
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)     # time step

data:
    # Primary solution fields, stored row-major: A[i,j] -> i * N + j
    u[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    v[i, j]: scratch DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # 1D temporaries for tridiagonal solves.
    # These are logically private to each independent line (column or row)
    # and can be allocated per worker/thread; they are not shared across
    # different (i, j) lines when those are run in parallel.
    p_col[i]: scratch DATA_TYPE      # length N, used in column sweep
    q_col[i]: scratch DATA_TYPE
    p_row[j]: scratch DATA_TYPE      # length N, used in row sweep
    q_row[j]: scratch DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    N: int
    TSTEPS: int

    DX: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 / N
    DY: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 / N
    DT: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 / TSTEPS
    B1: DATA_TYPE = 2.0
    B2: DATA_TYPE = 1.0

    mul1: DATA_TYPE = B1 * DT / (DX * DX)
    mul2: DATA_TYPE = B2 * DT / (DY * DY)

    a: DATA_TYPE = -mul1 / 2.0
    b: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 + mul1
    c: DATA_TYPE = a
    d: DATA_TYPE = -mul2 / 2.0
    e: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 + mul2
    f: DATA_TYPE = d

    # Precompute frequently used combinations to reduce flops.
    one_plus_2a: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 + 2.0 * a
    one_plus_2d: DATA_TYPE = 1.0 + 2.0 * d

    # Tunable blocking factors for outer (parallel) loops.
    TILE_ROW: int  # e.g. 32
    TILE_COL: int  # e.g. 32

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization: u[i][j] = (i + N - j) / N
    # Original C: u[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE)(i + n - j) / n;
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        u[i, j] = ( (DATA_TYPE)(i + N - j) ) / (DATA_TYPE)N

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Time-stepping loop: t = 0 .. TSTEPS-1
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    for t in seq(0, TSTEPS):
        # ============================
        # Column sweep (implicit in i)
        # ============================
        # For each interior column j, solve a tridiagonal system along i
        # to update v[:, j], with boundary v[0, j] = v[N-1, j] = 1.
        COL_SWEEP:
        for j in [1, N-1):     # j = 1 .. N-2
            # Boundary conditions and initial conditions for this column.
            v[0, j]  = (DATA_TYPE)1.0
            v[N-1, j] = (DATA_TYPE)1.0

            p_col[0] = (DATA_TYPE)0.0
            q_col[0] = v[0, j]      # == 1.0

            # Forward sweep along i (rows 1 .. N-2).
            FWD_COL:
            for i in seq(1, N-1):   # i = 1 .. N-2
                denom = a * p_col[i - 1] + b
                p_col[i] = -c / denom

                q_col[i] =
                    ( -d * u[i - 1, j]
                      + one_plus_2d * u[i, j]
                      - f * u[i + 1, j]
                      - a * q_col[i - 1] ) / denom

            # Back substitution along i (rows N-2 .. 1).
            # First the last interior point:
            v[N - 2, j] = p_col[N - 2] * v[N - 1, j] + q_col[N - 2]

            BWD_COL:
            for i in seq(N - 3, 0, -1):  # i = N-3 .. 1, descending
                v[i, j] = p_col[i] * v[i + 1, j] + q_col[i]

        # =========================
        # Row sweep (implicit in j)
        # =========================
        # For each interior row i, solve a tridiagonal system along j
        # to update u[i, :], with boundary u[i,0] = u[i,N-1] = 1.
        ROW_SWEEP:
        for i in [1, N-1):     # i = 1 .. N-2
            # Boundary conditions and initial conditions for this row.
            u[i, 0]   = (DATA_TYPE)1.0
            u[i, N-1] = (DATA_TYPE)1.0

            p_row[0] = (DATA_TYPE)0.0
            q_row[0] = u[i, 0]       # == 1.0

            # Forward sweep along j (columns 1 .. N-2).
            FWD_ROW:
            for j in seq(1, N-1):    # j = 1 .. N-2
                denom = d * p_row[j - 1] + e
                p_row[j] = -f / denom

                q_row[j] =
                    ( -a * v[i - 1, j]
                      + one_plus_2a * v[i, j]
                      - c * v[i + 1, j]
                      - d * q_row[j - 1] ) / denom

            # Back substitution along j (columns N-2 .. 1).
            u[i, N - 2] = p_row[N - 2] * u[i, N - 1] + q_row[N - 2]

            BWD_ROW:
            for j in seq(N - 3, 0, -1):  # j = N-3 .. 1, descending
                u[i, j] = p_row[j] * u[i, j + 1] + q_row[j]

optimization:
    # =======================
    # Parallelization strategy
    # =======================
    # Time steps are inherently sequential (each step depends on u, v from
    # the previous step), so keep t outer and sequential.

    # Column sweep: each column j is independent (given current u), so we
    # parallelize over blocks of columns. p_col and q_col are privatized per
    # worker (one 1D buffer of length N per worker).
    block(j, Jc, TILE_COL)          # split columns into tiles of size TILE_COL
    parallelize(Jc)                 # run tiles of columns in parallel

    # Row sweep: each row i is independent (given current v), so we
    # parallelize over blocks of rows. p_row and q_row are privatized per
    # worker (one 1D buffer of length N per worker).
    block(i, Ir, TILE_ROW)          # split rows into tiles of size TILE_ROW
    parallelize(Ir)                 # run tiles of rows in parallel

    # ======================
    # Locality & computation
    # ======================
    # Within each tridiagonal solve we access u or v along contiguous memory
    # in the inner loop (i for column sweep, j for row sweep), so we keep
    # those loops as the innermost sequential loops to maximize cache reuse.

    # Explicitly hoist t to be the outermost loop to reuse u/v in cache
    # across the column and row sweeps for a given time step.
    hoist(t)

    # Short unrolling of backward substitution loops to reduce loop overhead
    # and improve ILP in the recurrence (no cross-iteration parallelism).
    # These only apply to BWD_COL and BWD_ROW loops.
    unroll(i, 4)    # in BWD_COL
    unroll(j, 4)    # in BWD_ROW

    # =========================
    # Arithmetic simplifications
    # =========================
    # one_plus_2a and one_plus_2d are precomputed scalars used in the
    # forward sweeps, avoiding repeated evaluation of (1 + 2*a) and
    # (1 + 2*d) inside the inner loops.
    hoist(one_plus_2a)
    hoist(one_plus_2d)

    # =========================
    # Memory usage considerations
    # =========================
    # Compared to the original 2D p[i,j] and q[i,j] (O(N^2) each), we use
    # 1D temporaries p_col, q_col, p_row, q_row of size O(N) that are
    # reused per line. This reduces global memory footprint and improves
    # cache locality. When parallelized, each worker gets its own copy of
    # the 1D buffers, but total extra memory remains well below 50% of the
    # original 4 * N^2 DATA_TYPE storage for u, v, p, q.

domain:
    # N: problem size, TSTEPS: number of time steps
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)          # time dimension
    i: dim in [0, N)               # spatial index i (row)
    j: dim in [0, N)               # spatial index j (column)

data:
    # Main solution field u; only u is observed outside the kernel.
    # Row‑major layout: u[i, j] is at offset i * N + j.
    u[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # v is an intermediate field with the same layout as u.
    v[i, j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # p and q are only ever used along one spatial index at a time (per i),
    # so we store them as 1D scratch arrays indexed by j instead of full N×N.
    # This shrinks memory footprint and improves cache locality.
    p_row[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j
    q_row[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j

parameters:
    # Problem sizes
    N:       int        # spatial extent
    TSTEPS:  int        # number of time steps

    # Discretization and PDE coefficients (match original code)
    DX:   DATA_TYPE
    DY:   DATA_TYPE
    DT:   DATA_TYPE
    B1:   DATA_TYPE
    B2:   DATA_TYPE
    mul1: DATA_TYPE
    mul2: DATA_TYPE
    a:    DATA_TYPE
    b:    DATA_TYPE
    c:    DATA_TYPE
    d:    DATA_TYPE
    e:    DATA_TYPE
    f:    DATA_TYPE

    # Precombined constants to avoid recomputing inside loops
    one_plus_2d: DATA_TYPE    # = 1 + 2*d
    one_plus_2a: DATA_TYPE    # = 1 + 2*a

    # Tuning knobs for optimization (chosen for the target machine)
    TI:        int            # tile size in i, e.g. 64
    VEC_I:     int            # vector width along i, e.g. 8
    UNROLL_J:  int            # unroll factor in j, e.g. 4

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parameter initialization (outside time loop)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    DX   = 1.0 / cast<DATA_TYPE>(N)
    DY   = 1.0 / cast<DATA_TYPE>(N)
    DT   = 1.0 / cast<DATA_TYPE>(TSTEPS)
    B1   = 2.0
    B2   = 1.0
    mul1 = B1 * DT / (DX * DX)
    mul2 = B2 * DT / (DY * DY)

    a = -mul1 / 2.0
    b = 1.0 + mul1
    c = a
    d = -mul2 / 2.0
    e = 1.0 + mul2
    f = d

    one_plus_2d = 1.0 + 2.0 * d
    one_plus_2a = 1.0 + 2.0 * a

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization of u (matches init_array):
    #   u[i][j] = (i + N - j) / N
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        u[i, j] = (cast<DATA_TYPE>(i + N - j)) / cast<DATA_TYPE>(N)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # ADI time stepping
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    for t in seq(0, TSTEPS):
        # ==============================================================
        # 1) Column sweep: for each column index i, solve a tridiagonal
        #    system along j to update v[*, i].
        #
        #    Original C (conceptual):
        #      for i = 1 .. N-2:
        #        v[0][i] = 1; p[i][0] = 0; q[i][0] = v[0][i];
        #        for j = 1 .. N-2:
        #          p[i][j] = -c / (a * p[i][j-1] + b);
        #          q[i][j] = ( -d*u[j-1][i] + (1+2d)*u[j][i] - f*u[j+1][i]
        #                     - a*q[i][j-1] ) / (a * p[i][j-1] + b);
        #        v[N-1][i] = 1;
        #        for j = N-2 .. 1:
        #          v[j][i] = p[i][j] * v[j+1][i] + q[i][j];
        # ==============================================================
        for i in [1, N-1):
            # Boundary conditions for this column i
            v[0,    i] = 1.0
            v[N-1,  i] = 1.0

            # Initialize tridiagonal forward-sweep coefficients
            p_row[0] = 0.0
            q_row[0] = v[0, i]

            # Forward sweep along j: 1 .. N-2 (inclusive)
            for j in seq(1, N-1):
                denom = a * p_row[j - 1] + b
                p_row[j] = -c / denom

                num = -d * u[j - 1, i] \
                      + one_plus_2d * u[j, i] \
                      - f * u[j + 1, i] \
                      - a * q_row[j - 1]
                q_row[j] = num / denom

            # Backward substitution along j: N-2 .. 1 (inclusive)
            for j in seq(N - 2, 0, -1):
                v[j, i] = p_row[j] * v[j + 1, i] + q_row[j]

        # ==============================================================
        # 2) Row sweep: for each row index i, solve a tridiagonal system
        #    along j to update u[i, *] using v.
        #
        #    Original C (conceptual):
        #      for i = 1 .. N-2:
        #        u[i][0] = 1; p[i][0] = 0; q[i][0] = u[i][0];
        #        for j = 1 .. N-2:
        #          p[i][j] = -f / (d * p[i][j-1] + e);
        #          q[i][j] = ( -a*v[i-1][j] + (1+2a)*v[i][j] - c*v[i+1][j]
        #                     - d*q[i][j-1] ) / (d * p[i][j-1] + e);
        #        u[i][N-1] = 1;
        #        for j = N-2 .. 1:
        #          u[i][j] = p[i][j] * u[i][j+1] + q[i][j];
        # ==============================================================
        for i in [1, N-1):
            # Boundary conditions for this row i
            u[i, 0]     = 1.0
            u[i, N - 1] = 1.0

            # Initialize tridiagonal forward-sweep coefficients
            p_row[0] = 0.0
            q_row[0] = u[i, 0]

            # Forward sweep along j: 1 .. N-2 (inclusive)
            for j in seq(1, N-1):
                denom = d * p_row[j - 1] + e
                p_row[j] = -f / denom

                num = -a * v[i - 1, j] \
                      + one_plus_2a * v[i, j] \
                      - c * v[i + 1, j] \
                      - d * q_row[j - 1]
                q_row[j] = num / denom

            # Backward substitution along j: N-2 .. 1 (inclusive)
            for j in seq(N - 2, 0, -1):
                u[i, j] = p_row[j] * u[i, j + 1] + q_row[j]

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelism
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Each tridiagonal system along j is independent for different i,
    # within a fixed time step t. We cannot parallelize across t or j
    # (because of recurrences), but we *can* parallelize across i.
    #
    # We block i into tiles of size TI and parallelize the outer tile
    # index. This improves cache reuse and reduces scheduling overhead.
    block(i, I, TI)          # i = I * TI + i_inner, tile size TI
    parallelize(I)           # run tiles of i in parallel on different cores

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop interchange for better memory locality
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # In the forward/backward sweeps, the data dependencies are only
    # along j (each p_row[j] and q_row[j] depends on j-1; each v[j,*]
    # and u[* ,j] depends on j+1). There are no dependencies across i.
    #
    # We interchange loops so that the innermost loop is over i, which
    # is the stride‑1 dimension in row‑major layout. This makes accesses
    # to u, v, p_row, q_row contiguous in memory.
    #
    # Conceptually, for the four sweeps:
    #   for i: for j: ...  ==>  for j: for i: ...
    interchange(i, j)        # apply to all (i, j) sweeps where legal

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # After interchange, the innermost loops over i have no loop-carried
    # dependencies and operate on contiguous memory locations, so they
    # are suitable for SIMD. Vectorizing along i exploits x86 AVX/AVX2/AVX-512.
    vectorize(i, VEC_I)      # SIMD across independent tridiagonal systems

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Unrolling
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The recurrences along j are inherently sequential, but unrolling
    # by a small factor improves ILP and reduces branch/loop overhead.
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)      # unroll j in all forward/backward sweeps

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Hoisting invariants
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Constants a..f, one_plus_2d, one_plus_2a are loop-invariant and
    # already computed outside the loops. We conceptually hoist them to
    # avoid redundant computation, but an optimizing compiler will also
    # do this.
    hoist(t)                 # conceptually hoist invariant scalar expressions
                              # out of inner loops into the t loop preheader

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Data-structure optimization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # p_row and q_row are 1D instead of N×N. This reduces memory from
    # 4*N^2 (u, v, p, q) to ~2*N^2 + O(N) (u, v, p_row, q_row), which
    # is well within the 50% extra-memory constraint and improves cache
    # behavior. No observable semantics change because p and q were
    # only used as scratch storage along j for a single i at a time.
    # (No explicit directive; documented as a design choice.)

domain:
    # Spatial domain (square N x N grid)
    i: dim in [0, N)      # first spatial index (matches C's i)
    j: dim in [0, N)      # second spatial index (matches C's j)
    # Time-stepping domain
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS) # time index

data:
    # Main solution field, updated in-place every time step
    u[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Row-major: u[i][j] in C is stored at offset i*N + j

    # Temporary fields used inside each time step
    v[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Stores intermediate solution after the column sweep

    p[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Per-line temporary coefficient for tridiagonal solves

    q[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Per-line temporary right-hand side for tridiagonal solves

parameters:
    N:       int      # grid size in each dimension
    TSTEPS:  int      # number of time steps
    DX  = 1.0 / N
    DY  = 1.0 / N
    DT  = 1.0 / TSTEPS
    B1  = 2.0
    B2  = 1.0
    mul1 = B1 * DT / (DX * DX)
    mul2 = B2 * DT / (DY * DY)

    # ADI coefficients (constant over whole run)
    a = -mul1 / 2.0
    b = 1.0 + mul1
    c = a
    d = -mul2 / 2.0
    e = 1.0 + mul2
    f = d

    # Precompute values used in every inner iteration to reduce flops
    two_a = 2.0 * a
    two_d = 2.0 * d

    # Tunable optimization parameters (chosen per target machine)
    TI:  int  # tile size along i (number of lines per tile), e.g. 64 or 128
    TJ:  int  # optional tile size along j for cache blocking, e.g. 64
    VW:  int  # SIMD width (elements per vector), e.g. 8 for float AVX2, 4 for double

computation:
    # Time-stepping loop
    for t in seq(0, TSTEPS):

        # ------------------------------------------------------------
        # Column sweep: implicit step along j for each fixed i
        # (solve many independent tridiagonal systems indexed by i)
        # ------------------------------------------------------------

        for i in [1, N-1):
            # Boundary at j = 0:
            #   v[0][i] = 1
            #   p[i][0] = 0
            #   q[i][0] = v[0][i]
            v[0, i] = 1.0
            p[i, 0] = 0.0
            q[i, 0] = v[0, i]

            # Forward sweep in j: Thomas algorithm
            for j in seq(1, N-1):
                # denom = a * p[i][j-1] + b;
                denom = a * p[i, j-1] + b

                # p[i][j] = -c / denom;
                p[i, j] = -c / denom

                # q[i][j] =
                #   (-d * u[j-1][i]
                #    + (1 + 2*d) * u[j][i]
                #    - f * u[j+1][i]
                #    - a * q[i][j-1]) / denom;
                num = -d        * u[j-1, i] \
                      + (1.0 + two_d) * u[j,   i] \
                      - f        * u[j+1, i] \
                      - a        * q[i,   j-1]
                q[i, j] = num / denom

            # Boundary at j = N-1:
            #   v[N-1][i] = 1.0;
            v[N-1, i] = 1.0

            # Backward substitution in j (descending):
            for j in seq(N-2, 0, -1):   # j = N-2, ..., 1
                # v[j][i] = p[i][j] * v[j+1][i] + q[i][j];
                v[j, i] = p[i, j] * v[j+1, i] + q[i, j]

        # ------------------------------------------------------------
        # Row sweep: implicit step along i for each fixed j
        # (again, many independent tridiagonal systems, now indexed by j)
        # ------------------------------------------------------------

        for i in [1, N-1):
            # Boundary at j = 0:
            #   u[i][0] = 1.0;
            #   p[i][0] = 0.0;
            #   q[i][0] = u[i][0];
            u[i, 0] = 1.0
            p[i, 0] = 0.0
            q[i, 0] = u[i, 0]

            # Forward sweep in j:
            for j in seq(1, N-1):
                # denom = d * p[i][j-1] + e;
                denom = d * p[i, j-1] + e

                # p[i][j] = -f / denom;
                p[i, j] = -f / denom

                # q[i][j] =
                #   (-a * v[i-1][j]
                #    + (1 + 2*a) * v[i][j]
                #    - c * v[i+1][j]
                #    - d * q[i][j-1]) / denom;
                num = -a        * v[i-1, j] \
                      + (1.0 + two_a) * v[i,   j] \
                      - c        * v[i+1, j] \
                      - d        * q[i,   j-1]
                q[i, j] = num / denom

            # Boundary at j = N-1:
            #   u[i][N-1] = 1.0;
            u[i, N-1] = 1.0

            # Backward substitution in j (descending):
            for j in seq(N-2, 0, -1):   # j = N-2, ..., 1
                # u[i][j] = p[i][j] * u[i][j+1] + q[i][j];
                u[i, j] = p[i, j] * u[i, j+1] + q[i, j]

dependencies:
    # Within a single time step t:
    # - For fixed i, the column forward sweep at (i, j) depends on (i, j-1) via
    #   p[i, j-1] and q[i, j-1]; j must be processed in increasing order.
    # - The column backward sweep at (i, j) depends on v[j+1, i], so j must be
    #   processed in decreasing order.
    # - Different i values are independent in both column sweeps.
    #
    # - For fixed i, the row forward sweep at (i, j) depends on (i, j-1) via
    #   p[i, j-1] and q[i, j-1]; j must again be processed in increasing order.
    # - The row backward sweep at (i, j) depends on u[i, j+1], so j must be
    #   processed in decreasing order.
    # - Different i values are independent in both row sweeps.
    #
    # - Time step t+1 depends on the fully updated u from time step t; therefore
    #   the loop over t is strictly sequential.

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Improve arithmetic efficiency
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Hoist all scalar expressions that depend only on N or TSTEPS
    # (DX, DY, DT, mul1, mul2, a..f, two_a, two_d) outside the loops.
    # This ensures they are computed once per run (or at most once per t),
    # not inside (i, j) loops.
    hoist(t)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Exploit independence across lines (i) for parallelism and SIMD
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # The tridiagonal solves are along j, but each line index i is independent.
    # We keep j sequential (to respect the Thomas recurrences), and exploit
    # parallelism and vectorization across i.
    #
    # Step 2.1: Interchange i and j in the inner sweeps to make i the inner
    #           loop (more cache-friendly and better for SIMD).
    #           This is legal because p[i, j] and q[i, j] only depend on (i, j-1),
    #           not on any other i'.
    #
    # Column sweep:
    interchange(i, j)  # applied to both forward and backward sweeps of v/p/q
    # Row sweep:
    interchange(i, j)  # applied to both forward and backward sweeps of u/p/q

    # After interchange, all sweeps look like:
    #   for j in seq(...):
    #       for i in [1, N-1): ...  # i is the inner, independent dimension

    # Step 2.2: Tile (block) the independent dimension i into chunks of TI
    #           to balance cache reuse and parallel overhead.
    block(i, I, TI)     # i = I * TI + i_in_tile, with i_in_tile < TI

    # Step 2.3: Parallelize across I (groups of lines). Each worker processes
    #           a block of TI lines independently for both column and row sweeps.
    parallelize(I)

    # Step 2.4: Vectorize across the inner i dimension inside each tile.
    #           For each fixed j, we update VW adjacent lines (i) simultaneously.
    vectorize(i, VW)

    # The boundary-initialization loops over i have no j-dependence and can
    # also be parallelized and vectorized:
    parallelize(i)
    vectorize(i, VW)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Optional blocking in the recurrence dimension j
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # For very large N, the accesses u[j±1, i] and v[i±1, j] can benefit from
    # limiting the active j-range per worker so that multiple neighboring lines
    # (i) and their vertical neighbors stay in cache.
    #
    # We tile j with size TJ, but each tile still respects the ordering within
    # j (forward and backward), so correctness is preserved.
    block(j, J, TJ)
    hoist(J)  # keep the tile index outermost to maximize reuse of cache lines

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Unroll short inner loops in backward substitutions
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # The backward-substitution loops perform very simple recurrences. A small
    # unroll factor reduces loop control overhead and can help with latency
    # hiding without blowing up code size.
    #
    # Note: unrolling is applied to the inner i loop where it exists; the
    # recurrence along j remains strictly sequential.
    unroll(i, 2)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Summary of parallelism and data movement
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # - t is sequential due to data dependence between time steps.
    # - For each t, all lines i in [1, N-1) are independent in both column
    #   and row sweeps, so we:
    #     * tile i into blocks of TI,
    #     * run blocks I in parallel across threads,
    #     * vectorize across i inside each block,
    #   while keeping j as the sequential recurrence dimension.
    #
    # - No additional large arrays are introduced; p, q, u, and v are reused
    #   as in the original code, so peak memory usage stays within the same
    #   order (any scalar temporaries are negligible and well below +50%).
